thread.title: You Probably Bought Your iPhone With This Bank's Help. Its Stock Is Worth Buying, Too

title: You Probably Bought Your iPhone With This Bank's Help. Its Stock Is Worth Buying, Too
text:
You Probably Bought Your iPhone With This Bank’s Help. Its Stock Is Worth Buying, Too By Oct. 19, 2018 4:00 p.m. ET Order Reprints Casmic Lab Text size
Citizens Financial Group , a large regional bank based in Providence, R.I., has one of the hottest lending niches in the world. The bank is the exclusive financing partner for iPhones bought directly from Apple . With more than half of all iPhone buyers opting for installment plans, Citizens’ Apple portfolio has surged from zero in 2015 to about $1 billion early this year.
Initiatives like that are helping Citizens (ticker: CFG) post steady growth in its total book of loans at a time when many rivals are struggling for any growth at all. Stiff competition and rising interest rates will probably hold regional banks’ loan growth to less then 1% this year, but Citizens is on track for nearly 4%, says analyst Peter Winter of Wedbush Securities. And by all indications, the bank is adding those loans prudently and profitably.
Investors don’t seem to grasp how well things are going for Citizens. The bank’s shares have dropped 13% this year, compared with 6% for the KBW Bank Index. At a recent $36, Citizens now trades at 1.3 times its tangible book, or accounting, value, versus 1.8 times for regional banks as a group. All of which makes Citizens look like a bargain. Morgan Stanley analyst Ken Zerbe sees the shares heading to $51—a gain of more than 40% from its recent price. Plus, the stock offers a nice dividend yield of 3.1%.
Citizens, with a market value of $17 billion, is one of the 20 largest banks in the U.S., according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. With branches in 11 states in New England, the mid-Atlantic region, and the Midwest, it’s a formidable player in both consumer and commercial banking. Citizens At A Glance The market hasn’t given Citizens Financial Group, a large regional bank, any credit for strong loan growth and improving returns. E= Estimate Sources: Bloomberg; company reports
The bank was spun off from Royal Bank of Scotland in an initial public offering in 2014. After missteps leading up to the global financial crisis a decade ago, RBS had been bailed out by the British government, which ended up with a controlling stake. As a consequence, Citizens suffered from underinvestment.
But its fortunes have improved markedly under CEO Bruce Van Saun, a seasoned banker who has been in charge since 2013. He put Citizens on a strong financial footing, with high capital ratios, and carried out a successful recruiting drive. “He has been able to attract a lot of talent from other banks,” says Winter.
Van Saun, whose 35-year financial-services career included senior posts at Bank of New York Mellon and Deutsche Bank , sums up his game plan succinctly: “to deliver positive operating leverage, which means we are growing our revenues faster than our expenses.” Indeed, revenues in the first nine months of this year climbed by 7%, while noninterest expenses rose 4%.
It has made Citizens much more profitable than it used to be. Return on tangible common equity was 13.5%, as of Sept. 30, up from 4.3% in the third quarter of 2013 and closing in on the industry average of about 16%. The bank has consistently beaten earnings estimates since its IPO. Friday, it reported third-quarter profits of 91 cents a share, up from 68 cents a year earlier, beating the consensus of 89 cents.
So, what’s keeping the stock down? Some investors worry that Citizen’s loan growth could end badly when the economy finally turns down. That certainly happened to many growing banks in the past. But Citizens is hardly on an unsustainable tear. Its loan portfolio’s increase this year, though better than rivals’, has actually eased from last year’s 5.7% pace, and is expected to average 4.5% over the next two years. “They are growing loans in a very consistent way,” says Morgan Stanley’s Zerbe. And so far, credit quality is holding up well. Nonperforming loans total 0.73% of the entire portfolio, down from 0.85% a year earlier.
Another concern about Citizens is that it lags behind its peers in generating fee income, which can be more predictable than interest income from loans. Fees accounted for just 27% of Citizen’s third-quarter revenue, versus about 40% for its peer group.
But Citizen’s noninterest income, mostly fees, was up 9%, year over year, in the third quarter, and Van Saun is moving to boost it further. In August, he closed a $511 million acquisition of Franklin American Mortgage, significantly bolstering Citizens’ home-loan servicing business. Servicers earn steady fees by funneling homeowners’ monthly loan payments to investors’ mortgage securities.
All the while, Citizens continues to hone its lending strategy. It has moved away from dicey markets like auto loans and into promising niches like student-loan refinancing for young professionals. These borrowers are far less risky than students taking on debt while in school. Citizens held $8.7 billion of education loans as of Sept. 30, up 9%. Newsletter Sign-up
It’s also making a mark in unsecured merchant finance loans, like the program with Apple (AAPL). Citizens provides 24-month installment loans for iPhones sold directly by Apple; qualified customers can upgrade their phones after 12 payments.
Citizens has been revamping its commercial business, too, with nearly half of its loan portfolio now in that category. Targeting companies around the U.S. with annual sales up to $3 billion, it has added expertise in specialties like mergers-and-acquisitions advice and foreign exchange.
The heavy dose of commercial loans, which typically reset periodically, makes the bank fairly sensitive to interest-rate hikes, so it should benefit from more Federal Reserve tightening. Citizens’ net interest margin—the difference between the yields on loans and the cost of funds—has climbed to 3.19% from 3.05%.
There could be some more good news for investors. Analysts expect the bank’s dividend to hit 98 cents a share this year, 53% above last year’s payout, and then up to $1.31 next year. In sum, given Citizens’ prospects, its Apple connection, and modest share price, the stock offers a good chance for investors to dial up dollars.
